bp: A search results page is not just a list of answers. It is a small piece of public infrastructure that decides what a person notices first, what they trust enough to read, and whether they keep exploring. Traditional web search trained users to scan ranked links, especially the upper-left part of the page, then decide which source to open. AI Overviews change that object by putting a generated answer above the old list of links. This paper asks what happens to the human search process when that new block sits in the most valuable attention location. The practical question is not only whether users like the generated material. It is whether the page still supports inspection of sources, scrolling to traditional results, and the familiar scanning habits described in earlier search behavior research. The study uses eye tracking because the central object is attention itself: where people look, how strongly they engage, and what they pass over.
wh: The hard part is that search behavior is partly conscious and partly automatic. A person may say they checked the links, but their eyes may have spent most of the session on the generated answer. They may also intend to compare sources, yet the page layout can pull them toward whatever is placed first. AI Overviews create a new tension: they may reduce effort by summarizing information quickly, but they may also occupy the same visual territory that historically drew attention to top-ranked links. Measuring this is difficult because the interface change is not just a content change. It changes position, size, wording, and perceived authority all at once. The paper therefore has to separate engagement with GenAI content from older scanning habits, including the classic golden triangle pattern where the top-left area receives the most attention. It also has to ask whether users are willing to scroll past the generated block.
naive: A smart beginner would ask users after a search session whether AI Overviews changed their behavior. That would be cheap and direct, but it would miss much of the phenomenon. People often remember the result they used, not the order in which they inspected the page or how long their gaze rested on each area. Another beginner approach would count clicks on blue links. That also fails because looking is not the same as clicking. A user can read the overview carefully, glance at links for confirmation, and click nothing. Or they can click a link after already forming an answer from the overview. The paper needs a measure closer to attention than memory or clicks.
ap: The core idea is to treat the search page as a visual field whose parts compete for human attention. The researchers run a lab eye-tracking study in which users interact with search engines that place GenAI results above the traditionally ranked results, often called the ten blue links. They then measure how people engage with the generated block, whether they scroll beyond it, and how their scanning differs from older work on search result pages. The engagement scale adds a second view: not only where the eyes moved, but how users evaluated the experience. The central move is empirical rather than algorithmic. Instead of assuming that generated summaries either replace or merely supplement links, the study observes the page-level behavior directly. Its reported finding is mixed in an important way: users engage significantly more with GenAI content, yet the golden triangle remains valid and blue-link behavior remains consistent with prior literature.
mech: The mechanism starts with a controlled search setting. Participants are placed in a lab where an eye-tracking setup can record gaze as they use a search interface containing a GenAI result above the ranked links. The input is a sequence of user interactions with the page: eye positions over time, scrolling behavior, engagement ratings, and likely ordinary interface actions such as viewing and moving through results. The page itself is divided conceptually into regions: the generated overview area, the traditional link area, and especially the upper-left zone that older search studies found to attract attention. The study then compares how much attention each region receives and whether users move past the generated content to inspect the links below. The transformation is from raw gaze and interaction traces into behavioral evidence: dwell patterns, scanning paths, willingness to scroll, and engagement scores. The comparison is against existing knowledge about search engine result page scanning, including the golden triangle and established blue-link patterns. The output is not a new ranking method. It is a characterization of changed behavior: GenAI content draws significantly more engagement, but it does not erase older scanning behavior. Users still engage with traditional ranked results in ways that match the literature.
math: The mathematical ideas here are measurement, comparison, and uncertainty from controlled observation. Eye tracking turns a continuous stream of gaze locations into counts and durations tied to page regions. In plain terms, it asks: out of all the moments in a search session, how many were spent looking at the overview, the links, or the upper-left area? That is a measurement problem because attention is invisible unless the study chooses observable traces that stand in for it. The engagement scale is another measurement device: it converts a user's experience into ordered responses that can be compared across people. The comparison principle is simple but important. To say AI Overviews change behavior, the study needs to compare observed patterns with earlier search-page patterns, especially the expectation that attention concentrates near the top-left and then spreads through ranked results. Probability enters because the researchers see a sample of users, not every searcher. A significant difference means the observed extra engagement with GenAI content is large enough, relative to variation among participants, that it is unlikely to be mere noise. The tradeoff is control versus naturalness. A lab study gives cleaner measurement of gaze, but it may not capture all habits, distractions, topics, and device contexts of everyday search.
dots: This paper sits in the repo's information-retrieval and search family, where the shared question is how people find useful information from a page that can show only a small ordered set. It connects to ranking because page position matters: a result above the links receives attention before lower candidates have a chance to compete. It connects to learning from examples and comparison because the study learns from observed user traces rather than from a hand-written theory of how searchers behave. In the same batch, Understanding and Modeling Heterogeneous Search Behavior studies how age, gender, language proficiency, tasks, logs, and interviews shape query and session behavior. The Search to Ask to Act keynote frames a broader shift from retrieving documents toward generated answers and agents. This paper studies the human side of that shift: when a search interface answers before listing sources, the user's attention path changes.
ww: The approach works because the suspected change is visual and behavioral, so a visual behavioral instrument is appropriate. If GenAI content really pulls attention away from links, that should appear in where eyes land, how long they stay, and whether users scroll. Self-report alone would blur these stages together, while click logs would ignore reading without clicking. Eye tracking gives a closer record of the searcher's inspection process. The study is also well matched to the historical question because older search research already describes recurring scanning patterns. That gives the new measurements a reference point: the paper can ask whether AI Overviews replace, weaken, or coexist with the golden triangle and blue-link behavior. The finding that users engage more with GenAI content but still show traditional patterns is plausible because the overview and the top-left area reinforce each other. The new content is placed where attention already tends to go. At the same time, searchers have learned to inspect ranked links, especially when they want sources, alternatives, or confirmation. The method can reveal coexistence rather than forcing a yes-or-no answer.
po: The payoff is a clearer picture of what AI Overviews are doing to search behavior. Grounded in the abstract, the study shows that GenAI content changes engagement: users interact with it significantly more. At the same time, the traditional golden triangle remains valid, and searchers still engage with blue links in patterns consistent with earlier literature. For search interface design, that matters because the overview is not a neutral add-on. It competes for prime attention while leaving some older source-inspection habits intact. The paper also outlines future directions for studying search behavior as GenAI becomes a standard page element.
limits: The abstract supports caution. This is a lab eye-tracking study, so the evidence is strong for controlled attention patterns but may not fully represent everyday search across devices, tasks, time pressure, or private needs. The abstract does not specify participant diversity, task types, query topics, exact interface variants, sample size, or whether the overview content was always correct. Eye gaze also indicates attention, not trust, understanding, or final decision quality by itself. The claim that GenAI changes behavior depends on the study's interface matching real search engines closely enough. The work shows engagement patterns, but it does not prove long-term effects on knowledge, source checking, misinformation exposure, or user dependence on generated answers.
